title: Real Estate Role in Job Creation in the US
text: Real Estate Role in Job Creation in the US Hsieh and Moretti (2003): when the average price of land in a city increases, the fraction of real estate brokers in a city increases, the productivity of an average real estate agent (houses sold per hour worked) falls, and the real wage of a typical real estate agent remains unchanged. 6 Source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics (seasonally adjusted; series CES2000000001 construction, CES5500000001 financial activities including real estate, CES0000000001 total nonfarm), author's calculation from December to December (end June for 2006). Earlier version: Credit Suisse, Exhibit 57. Hsieh, C.-T. and Moretti, E. (2003), Journal of Political Economy, 111(5), 1076–1122. Higher land prices draw in more brokers, but not more productive or better-paid ones, so a boom adds cost, not output. If talent keeps flowing towards real estate, what happens to growth in the rest of the economy? Construction, finance and real estate: share of US nonfarm job additions

title: Allocation of Productive vs Rent-Seeking Activities in an Economy
text: Allocation of Productive vs Rent-Seeking Activities in an Economy Payoffs against n, the ratio of rent-seekers to market producers. α: payoff to market production when nothing is expropriated; γ: payoff to subsistence production, which cannot be expropriated, so it is the floor below which producers will not go; β: the most a rent-seeker can take, a limit set by the rent-seeker's own technology. 7a Source: Murphy, K.M., Shleifer, A. and Vishny, R.W. (1993), "Why is rent-seeking so costly to growth?", American Economic Review (Papers and Proceedings) 83(2), 409–414, Figures 1 to 3 (pages 410 and 411). β < γ (Figure 1): property rights are well protected, rent-seeking pays less than subsistence, and everyone produces for the market. A unique equilibrium, with income per head α. β > α (Figure 2): rent-seeking beats market production, so rent-seekers crowd in until the payoff to production has fallen to γ. A unique, bad equilibrium: income per head is γ. γ < β < α (Figure 3): two stable equilibria, a good one with no rent-seekers and a bad one with n = n″.

title: The Four Quadrants in Long-run Equilibrium
text: The Four Quadrants in Long-run Equilibrium Reading anticlockwise from the north-east rent is determined in the space market capitalised into a price the price calls forth construction, and construction replaces the stock that rent was determined on. Equilibrium requires that the path returns to where it began. After DiPasquale, D. and Wheaton, W.C. (1992) "The markets for real estate assets and space: a conceptual framework", Real Estate Economics, 20(2), 181–197; see Wheaton, W.C. (2008) MIT OpenCourseWare 11.433J/15.021J, week 1. Curves redrawn in the constant-elasticity form of equations (1) and (3). 11 Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4

title: Demand Growth in the Space Market
text: Demand Growth in the Space Market Employment rises, so the demand schedule for space shifts out. The stock cannot change immediately, so rent must absorb the whole of the shock, and only later does new building take the pressure off. Short run: rent jumps along D1 to the spike R1, at the old stock. Price follows rent up the valuation line, because P = R/i and the cap rate i has not moved. The higher price lifts construction above the replacement rate, so the stock starts to grow. A larger stock moves the market back down D1: rent falls from the spike but settles above its starting level. Long run: rent, price, stock and construction all end higher than before. The more readily building responds to price, the smaller the spike and the larger the extra stock. After DiPasquale, D. and Wheaton, W.C. (1992) "The markets for real estate assets and space: a conceptual framework", Real Estate Economics, 20(2), 181–197; see Wheaton, W.C. (2008) MIT OpenCourseWare 11.433J/15.021J, week 1. Curves redrawn in the constant-elasticity form of equations (1) and (3). 12

title: Yield Compression in the Asset Market
text: Yield Compression in the Asset Market The capitalisation rate falls (from 11 to 8 per cent in the figure), so the valuation line flattens and the same rent supports a higher price. The shock arrives from the capital market rather than from occupiers, and its effect on rent runs in the opposite direction. Short run: price jumps to P1 at the old rent, because rent cannot change until the stock does. The higher price lifts construction above the replacement rate, so the stock grows. A larger stock moves the market down the unchanged demand curve D0, so rent falls. Long run: price and stock end higher and rent ends lower. Price settles below the impact price P1, because falling rent gives back part of the gain. Compare the demand shock on the previous slide: there rent and price move together, here they move in opposite directions. After DiPasquale, D. and Wheaton, W.C. (1992) "The markets for real estate assets and space: a conceptual framework", Real Estate Economics, 20(2), 181–197; see Wheaton, W.C. (2008) MIT OpenCourseWare 11.433J/15.021J, week 1. Curves redrawn in the constant-elasticity form of equations (1) and (3). 13

title: The Quadrant Model with a Long-run Supply Curve
text: The Quadrant Model with a Long-run Supply Curve Source: Colwell, P.F. (2002) "Tweaking the DiPasquale–Wheaton model", Journal of Housing Economics, 11(1), 24–39, Figure 2 ("Adding long-run supply"), DOI 10.1006/jhec.2001.0301; redrawn. 15 Colwell (2002) adds a long-run supply curve (LRS) to the four-quadrant model. LRS shows how long-run equilibrium is found, the first point of the critique on slide 14. LRS slopes upwards: a higher rent supports more building and a larger stock. A demand increase leaves LRS where it is and moves the market along it: stock and rent both rise. More building supply shifts LRS out (stock up, rent down). A higher depreciation rate, operating-expense ratio or cap rate shifts it in (stock down, rent up).

title: Observations and Assumptions: Cambridge 2022
text: Observations and Assumptions: Cambridge 2022 The rent, the price and the valuation line connecting them are observed: £15,960 a year, £537,906, and a cap rate of 2.97% for Cambridge in 2022. The stock is set to 100 in the base year and construction to the replacement rate, because neither is in the data. The base year is assumed to be in long-run equilibrium, so the rectangle closes: that rent supports that price, that price sustains replacement building, and that building holds the stock at 100. The demand and construction curves pass through the observed point; their slopes depend on the elasticities ε and β, which are assumed. So the model can say by what per cent rent, price and stock change after a shock, but not the level of the stock or of construction. The next two slides shock this base year. Rent and price observed (advertised rents, Rightmove; sold prices, HM Land Registry; geometric means, Cambridge, 2022; author's calculations; stock and construction indexed). 16

title: Scenario 1: A Demand Shock
text: Scenario 1: A Demand Shock Search enquiries for Cambridge fell by about 20% between 2021 and 2023. With a fall in the demand for space, the model says rent should collapse on impact to £9,136. On impact the stock is fixed, so rent absorbs the whole shock: £9,136 is 43 per cent below the base (£15,960). Price follows at the unchanged cap rate, to £307,915. Below-base prices push construction under the replacement rate, so the stock shrinks to 88.3. Rent recovers to £12,455, 22 per cent below the base, and price to £419,787. Advertised rents in Cambridge actually rose by 18.9 per cent between 2022 and 2025, so the model is wrong in sign as well as in size. A gap this wide points to a wrong assumption, not necessarily a failed model: supply and yields did not stand still. Demand shift from search enquiries; ε = 0.4, β = 0.5. Observed rent change: advertised rents, Rightmove, Cambridge (geometric mean), 2022 to 2025; author's calculations. 17

title: Scenario 2: A Shock from the Asset Market
text: Scenario 2: A Shock from the Asset Market Capitalisation rate changed from 2.97% to 3.72%. Price falls on impact to £429,371, building falls with it, the stock drifts down to 95.1, and rent rises to £18,089. On impact rent is unchanged and price falls by 20%. Lower prices put construction under the replacement rate, so the stock shrinks by 4.9%. The smaller stock lifts rent by 13%, and price recovers part of its fall to £486,639, 9.5% below the base. This mirrors yield compression on slide 13: there price, stock and building rise and rent falls; here price, stock and building fall and rent rises. 18

title: Summary of the Cambridge 2022 Case
text: Summary of the Cambridge 2022 Case Short run: the year of the shock, with the stock still at its base level of 100. Nothing can be built yet, so a demand shock lands on rent and a yield shock lands on price. Long run: the stock has fully adjusted and construction again equals replacement, so the rectangle closes at a new point. The percentages are changes from the base. Summary: a fall in demand cuts rent and price in both runs, while a rise in the cap rate cuts price in both runs but raises rent in the long run, because the smaller stock is scarcer. 19 Quadrant variable Base, Cambridge 2022 Scenario 1: demand for space falls 20% Scenario 2: cap rate rises 75 basis points Short run Long run Short run Long run Rent, £ per year £15,960 £9,136 (−43%) £12,455 (−22%) £15,960 £18,089 (+13%) Price per dwelling £537,906 £307,915 (−43%) £419,787 (−22%) £429,371 (−20%) £486,639 (−10%) Stock, index 100.0 100.0 88.3 (−12%) 100.0 95.1 (−5%) Construction per year, % of base stock 1.50 1.13 (−24%) 1.33 (−12%) 1.34 (−11%) 1.43 (−5%) Capitalisation rate 2.97% 2.97% 2.97% 3.72% 3.72%
